column5: skin as clothing; bones and sinews knit together
column6: The commentary combines tightly woven fabric with the place where bones meet; Job addresses God as the one who clothed him with skin and flesh and knit him together with bones and sinews, giving both images one bodily setting.

The source's حق can mean where two bones meet and its counsel joins separated pieces; Ezekiel reports that at the prophetic word the scattered bones came together, bone to its bone, before the bodies lived.

column5: dry bones; lost hope; cut off
column6: The commentary sets joining and repair against loss and severance; the exiles identify themselves as dry bones and say their hope is lost and they are cut off, making the physical reunion of verse 7 answer a declared communal loss.

The commentary puts tightly woven fabric beside the meeting of bones; the psalmist describes his bodily frame as intricately woven while hidden in formation, a creation image rather than a moral construction.

column5: two workers and reward for toil
column6: The commentary makes mutual joining and useful work answer loss; Ecclesiastes says two are better than one because their labor has a good reward, grounding the lifting and unbreakable cord described in the following verses.

column5: iron sharpens iron; person sharpens person
column6: The commentary's tavsiye is reciprocal counsel that strengthens a structure; Proverbs describes one person sharpening another as iron sharpens iron, making mutual improvement a material image.
The commentary distinguishes the sound foundation from the one that collapses; the psalm asks what the righteous can do if foundations are destroyed, making structural failure an ethical crisis.

The commentary defines صالح as repairing damage and presents a secure house as its product; God promises to raise David's fallen booth and repair its breaches, making restoration of a ruined dwelling explicit.

column5: ع م ل / Hebrew עמל, table sound correspondence
column6: The commentary asks whether work can answer loss through righteousness; Isaiah's servant comes through the toil of his soul to an outcome that makes many righteous, linking the cognate for painful effort to a fruitful result in this verse's own servant context.

column5: ح ق ق / Hebrew חקק, table sound correspondence
column6: The source sets firm حق beside a covenant that can be broken; Jeremiah says that if God's fixed cosmic statutes depart, Israel will cease as a people, using the cognate for enduring ordinances to secure the restored relationship.

column5: hearts encouraged and knit together in love
column6: The commentary makes reciprocal counsel join parts into one whole; Paul seeks encouraged hearts joined together in love as they reach assured understanding, giving verbal support and cohesion one purpose.
The commentary joins firm truthful speech to constructive works; the letter urges love in deed and truth rather than words alone, making both elements necessary to a real bond.

column5: persist in doing good until harvest
column6: The ayah joins good deeds with mutual counsel in patience; Galatians tells the community not to tire of doing good because a harvest comes if they do not give up, giving endurance a concrete gain.
The commentary opposes durable, beneficial work to loss; Paul calls believers steadfast and abundant in the Lord's work because their labor is not vain, joining firmness, work, and gain.

column5: do not tire of doing good
column6: The commentary makes righteous work something held together by patience; the letter directly tells brothers not to grow weary in doing good, identifying fatigue as a threat to the work.

The surah names good deeds and patient exhortation as the exception to loss; Paul describes those who persist in good work seeking glory and receiving eternal life, linking sustained action to its outcome.
The source's woven fabric and joined bones picture sound formation; the psalmist says God knit him in his mother's womb, giving the textile image a personal bodily origin.

The commentary treats joined pieces as part of restoration; Ezekiel sees sinews, flesh, and skin cover the assembled bones, yet says there is no breath in them, qualifying how far physical reconstruction alone goes.

The commentary wants labor to yield a durable structure rather than loss under time; the prayer asks God to establish the work of human hands, directly turning transient toil into a request for permanence.

column5: unjust house built with unpaid labor
column6: The source uses a builder's bricklaying for صالح deeds; Jeremiah condemns the man who builds his house unjustly by making a neighbor work without wages, showing that successful construction can embody corruption.

column5: stone houses built but not inhabited
column6: The commentary contrasts sound building with loss; Amos tells oppressors that although they built houses of dressed stone they will not live in them, linking unjust work to forfeited shelter.
The commentary's joined building signifies beneficial action; Habakkuk pronounces woe on the person who builds a town with blood, making the shared construction harmful through its means.

column5: peoples labor for fire and nothing
column6: The commentary sets constructive work against loss; the next verse says peoples toil only for fire and weary themselves for nothing, giving the unjust city's building its fruitless end.
The earlier Babel scene joins people around brickmaking and a tower; God disperses the builders over the earth, completing the counterexample to the commentary's beneficial joining.

column5: hands lay foundation and finish house
column6: The commentary's work places bricks into a sound whole; Zechariah says Zerubbabel's hands laid the temple foundation and will complete it, keeping beginning and completion in the same laboring hands.

column5: rebuild ruins and repair devastated cities
column6: The commentary describes صالح as repair after spoilage; Isaiah says the restored people will rebuild ancient ruins and repair devastated cities, making collective recovery a construction task.

The commentary gives حق the force of something firm and rightly set; the psalm joins God's everlasting righteousness to instruction that is truth, linking durability and moral truth without the fabric metaphor.
The source calls a well-formed utterance firm; the psalm says the sum of God's word is truth and every righteous judgment endures, locating verbal soundness in permanence.

The source compares sound speech with a door's foot fitting its socket; Proverbs likens a word spoken at the right time to gold apples in silver settings, giving apt placement an image of material fit.

column5: wise rebuke fitted to listening ear
column6: The commentary's counsel must attach person to person; Proverbs pairs a wise reprover with an ear that listens, comparing the encounter to a gold ornament, so the fit depends on receiving speech.

The commentary quotes a divine covenant broken after being bound; Zechariah enacts the opposite direction when the shepherd breaks his staff and thereby annuls his covenant, making the actor and direction of rupture distinct.
The commentary says cutting what ought to be joined leads to loss; the shepherd breaks a second staff to annul the brotherhood between Judah and Israel, an enacted severance of a social bond.

The commentary insists that firm words become useful through deeds; this teaching says practice is the main thing rather than exposition and cautions against multiplying words, sharpening the distinction between sound speech and empty talk.
The commentary's reciprocal joining must endure strain; Ephesians asks believers to bear with one another in love with humility, gentleness, and patience before urging unity.

column5: unity kept in a bond of peace
column6: The source says recommendation attaches one part to another; Ephesians directs believers to maintain the Spirit's unity in the bond of peace, expressing an ethical joining before its jointed-body image.
The commentary turns individual works into a collective building; Paul calls his fellow ministers God's coworkers and the community God's building, identifying both laborers and structure.
The source compares secure and collapsing foundations; Paul says no one can lay a foundation other than Jesus Christ, specifying why the community's building can be sound.

The commentary's firm fabric and sound bricks imply that materials matter; Paul lists lasting and combustible materials a builder might place on the foundation, preparing for the fire test in the next verse.
The ayah names patience alongside good action; Hebrews says believers need endurance so that, having done God's will, they receive the promise, tying perseverance to completed action.

column5: do good especially to faith's household
column6: The commentary treats righteous work as building a community; Galatians urges doing good to everyone, especially the household of faith, identifying the circle in which the work strengthens bonds.

The commentary's building holds only when its joined pieces are sound; Hermas's tower vision sets rejected stones beside stones incorporated into it, making the fitness of each component morally consequential.

column5: small and great bodily members together
column6: The source compares mutual counsel to parts joined in a body; Clement's discussion of members says the body requires both small and great parts to function together, extending the anatomical image to church order.

The commentary's good deeds attach people and repair what is weak; Clement asks strong members to care for weak members and rich ones to supply the poor, giving the jointed body a practical obligation.

column5: believers as stones of Father's temple
column6: The commentary builds a sound structure from its believers' deeds; Ignatius pictures his addressees as stones of the Father's temple raised by the cross, with faith and love involved in their movement.
